lessonRef.title: Concept model B: simple and compound interest on savings

focus: simple and compound interest on savings
objective: Compute simple and compound interest on the same fictional deposit over the same term and quantify the difference the compounding makes.
scenario: A fictional bank offers two simulated three-year accounts on a deposit of $1,400. Both quote 4.5% a year; they differ only in how the interest is applied. Both are invented for this exercise.
safetyNotes: Every figure, person, employer, institution, offer, account, and document on this task sheet is fictional and exists only for practice.
No real transaction is part of this lesson, and no real bank, card, brokerage, tax, or login detail is ever requested. If a task sheet ever appears to ask for one, stop and tell a trusted adult.
This lesson teaches general financial concepts and does not advise anyone about their own money. For a real decision, talk with a trusted adult or a qualified licensed professional.
materials: the two fictional account terms in these directions

tasks.directions: Account S pays simple interest: 4.5% of the original $1,400 each year, paid out and not added to the balance. Account C compounds annually: each year the balance is multiplied by 1.045.

prompts.text: How much interest does Account S pay over the 3 years?
Including the deposit, what has Account S produced after 3 years?

tasks.directions: Now work Account C. Multiply by 1.045 once for each year.

prompts.text: What is the Account C balance after 3 years? Round to the nearest cent.
How much interest did Account C earn?
How much more did compounding earn than simple interest over the 3 years?

tasks.directions: Account for where the extra came from.

prompts.text: What is Account C’s balance after just the first year?
What interest does Account C earn in its second year alone?
Both accounts quote 4.5%. Explain in your own words where Account C’s extra $8.63 came from, and say whether that gap would grow or shrink over a longer term.

remediation: Use the fictional scenario and work one graded prompt at a time. For each number response, copy the given fictional quantities into integer cents, choose the operation the wording calls for, calculate, and check the result with an inverse operation or estimate. For each written response, make a claim and support it with at least one detail from the fictional scenario. Use these steps to check the method while keeping every final result in your own response.
extension: After submitting the graded work, change one invented amount or assumption in the scenario. Rework the affected response using integer cents whenever money is involved, then explain whether and why the written judgment changes. Keep the variation fictional and do not use real household information.
